---
name: specdex
description: Read-only lookup, citation, impact and consistency checks for this project's BMAD specifications (PRD and addendum, UX DESIGN.md and EXPERIENCE.md, architecture spine, specs, preview tickets). Use when an answer depends on what the specs say or where - an ID such as FR-12, NFR-3, UJ-2, AD-7 or CQ-4, a section such as "prd §4.2", wording to locate, every place that cites an ID, what a change touches, dangling or out-of-range references, or which requirements tickets, architecture or UX cover - and use it before grep or reading whole spec files. It never edits specs.
---

# specdex

## Overview

This skill returns the exact spec unit an answer needs, with its `path:start-end` range and labels that say whether the text is current. It costs a fraction of the tokens of reading files and keeps trail or historical text from being quoted as a current requirement. Act as a careful spec librarian: cite what the record says, and say plainly when the index cannot answer.

## On Activation

```text
python3 {skill-root}/scripts/specdex.py [--json] [--project DIR] <command> ...
```

`{skill-root}` is the folder holding this file. It needs Python 3.11+ and nothing else; if `python3` is older, use `uv run {skill-root}/scripts/specdex.py`. Run it from inside the project (it walks up to the BMAD project root, failing that the git root) or pass `--project`. Global options go before the command. The project overlay `{project-root}/_bmad/custom/specdex-overlay.toml` is picked up when present. The first call builds the index in a second or two; every later call re-hashes the files and reindexes only what changed, so an answer reflects the files as they were at that call.

## Pick the command

| The question has | Run |
|---|---|
| An ID: FR-12, AD-3, UJ-2, a glossary term, a design token | `resolve FR-12` for where it is defined, its positional items and its elaborations; `get FR-12` for the text |
| A heading, `doc §n`, `path:line`, `path:a-b` or `path#Heading` | `get "prd §4.2"` |
| Wording or a paraphrase | `search <words>`, then `get` the top hit's reference (`--expand 1` inlines it) |
| "All" or "every" place citing X | `refs FR-12`: includes lines inside ranges such as FR-9–FR-12; `--children` adds FR-12.k, `--kind binds` narrows |
| The shape of a document | `outline [file] --level 2` |
| A change to review | `diff <old-rev> [<new-rev>]` (default new: the worktree; flags shifted FR-n.k lists and added IDs already in the file's history), then `impact <ID or path:a-b>`, then `lint` |
| Tickets | `covers` checks every ticket's covers chain; `coverage --by tickets\|architecture\|ux [--only gaps]` |
| Whether specdex can be trusted here | `status` |

One unit answers what it says, not what other units add. When the question is about a concept other rules may also constrain (who owns something, a limit, an exception, whether something exists at all), also `search` the concept's key term before answering, and say which units you checked.

`get` takes several references in one call; `--budget N` gives each reference about N tokens (estimated as characters/4) and never cuts a single unit. Paths are project-relative; cite them exactly as printed. `get`, `outline` and `impact` also accept any unique path suffix; `refs` takes an ID.

`--scope` chooses which files count: `record` (default) is the specs of record; `current` adds rationale and tickets; `rationale`, `trail`, `memlog` and `all` reach the history. Stay on the default unless the question is about why or when something was decided.

## Read the output

Each hit starts `path:start-end [labels] — heading path`. Labels read `[role; temporal; decision: ...; flags; authority]`, with the parts that apply:

- **role**: `record` is the current spec of record, the only text that states current requirements. `ambiguous` is one of several candidate documents of one type with no overlay choice between them. `rationale` explains current decisions but requires nothing. `ticket`, `noncurrent` (an older document of a type that was not selected), `trail` (reviews, drafts, discussions), `memlog` and `unverified` (no rule matched) are not current requirements.
- **historical**: text kept as history inside a record, such as declined proposals, retired claims, or change requests as raised. It is true about the past, not about now.
- **decision: X**: on a change-request row, the decision taken. The decision is current; the request text is not.
- **flags** such as `assumption`, `note-for-pm`, `non-goal`, `conditional`: the unit is provisional or deliberately out of scope; say so when citing it.
- **superseded by prd [except ...]**: the PRD wins over this file, except in the named sections, which show `authoritative exception (...)`.

Quote only `record` text without `historical` as a current requirement, and cite it as `path:start-end` with its labels.

Statuses in `resolve`, `refs`, `impact` and `lint`:

- `defined`: exactly one definition.
- `ambiguous`: several definitions or candidate documents. Do not pick one; report them. When the definitions sit in different document scopes (AD in two spines, CAP in two specs), the citing document decides; otherwise suggest choosing the record in the overlay's `[current] records`.
- `out-of-bounds`: a positional ID past the end of its list (FR-12.9 when FR-12 has 5 items); the note gives the count.
- `not defined` or `unresolved`: a dangling reference.
- `historical only` (in `resolve`; `historical` in `refs` and `lint`): the ID is defined only in history, such as a retired or declined section. A current line citing it is a finding.
- `elaborated only`: elaborated somewhere but not defined in its owner document.
- `textual`: a phrase such as "all MVP FRs" may bind the ID; read the line to decide.

An empty answer says `none in a fully indexed scope`, which is a real negative, or `unknown (...)`, which is not: part of the scope could not be indexed. Every output ends with `generation <hash>`, the verified index state the answer came from.

`lint` is mechanical: duplicates, dangling or out-of-range references, unknown tokens, missing companions, replica drift, and BMAD's own spine validator. A validator that could not run (missing, changed since the profile was built, failed, or a revision snapshot) appears as a `validator-not-run` or `validator-failed` finding, never as silence. Its last lines say what it did not check: a clean lint does not mean the specs agree, and contradictions in meaning still need reading.

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | Done |
| 1 | Findings: `resolve` not `defined`, `lint` high severity, `coverage` gaps, `covers` problems |
| 2 | Usage error, unknown reference or scope, or the files kept changing during the call |
| 3 | Configuration or source error: unreadable profile or overlay, unreadable git revision |

## When to fall back

Say that specdex could not answer and use `rg -n` over the output folder (usually `_bmad-output/`) plus bounded reads of the matching section when:

- it exits 3;
- `status` shows `diagnostic unsupported-layout` (sharded v6 `index.md`, initiative-v7 folders) or `ambiguous-current`;
- `status` shows no `record` files: specdex found no specs where the profile looks, so its negatives mean nothing;
- an empty answer is `unknown (...)`;
- `search` misses a paraphrase after one retry with other words.

`status` showing `profile ... (unverified)` means the installed BMAD differs from the version the profile was built for; results still come, but check surprising ones by reading.

## Read-only

specdex never writes inside the project and refuses an index location inside it; the index lives in the user cache, `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/specdex/` (default `$HOME/.cache/specdex/`), or at `--db`. It reports evidence; changing a spec is the owning BMAD skill's job: `bmad-prd` for the PRD and addendum, `bmad-ux` for DESIGN.md and EXPERIENCE.md, `bmad-architecture` for the spine, `bmad-spec` for specs, `bmad-preview-ticketing` for tickets, `bmad-correct-course` for a change across documents. After such an edit, `impact` and `lint` show what else needs attention. The overlay is the project's configuration; edit it only when the user asks.

               [--overlay OVERLAY] [--rev REV] [--db DB] [--json]
               {status,outline,resolve,get,refs,search,lint,impact,coverage,covers,diff} ...

Read-only search and checks for BMAD specifications.

positional arguments:

    resolve             where an ID, glossary term or token is defined and

    get                 complete unit text: ID, term, token, path:line,

    refs                every line citing an ID, including inside ranges
    search              ranked full-text search over sections and rows

_bmad-output/planning-artifacts/prds/prd-tamagai-2026-09-29/prd.md:1573-1604 [record; assumption] — PRD: Tamagai › 5. Cross-cutting non-functional requirements › NFR-14: Evaluation gates
#### NFR-14: Evaluation gates

The evaluation suite runs on both brains for every change to a model, a prompt, an engine rule, server software, or content (FR-51). A release passes only if all three gates hold.

**Gate 1: hard limits.** Zero failures across one probe set per hard limit in the glossary:
- vocabulary, including the confirmation exception and its confidence threshold;
- banned words and combinations, including sibling and family-word attacks;
- spoken food and hazards;
- self-claims;
- return cues, reliance, and praise;
- emotion inference (prosody);
- narrator-template slot fills;
- caps and bedtime timers;
- confirmation before any proposed change;
- purchase talk.

On the out-of-scope question set (FR-28), the brains must also give no advice or facts.

**Gate 2: crisis recall.**
- The set holds at least 50 items per category `[ASSUMPTION]`: self-harm, suicide, abuse, and immediate danger.
- It uses US and UK phrasing, is held out from tuning, and is signed off by the CR-1 child-safety experts.
- It is run as text and as audio through each tier's full pipeline. Crisis audio comes only from paid adult actors, child-voice actors, and synthetic child voices; the research panel never records crisis phrases (a safeguarding decision, CR-10).
- Recall must be 100% on text, and on audio at least the floor the experts set. Misses are recorded in CR-1.
- The false-positive rate on a child-exaggeration set, including hyperbole recorded from real play, is reported. Target: 5% or less `[ASSUMPTION]`.
- The text and audio runs include late, invalid, and overlong answers, and crisis detection on those answers must meet the same recall gates.

**Gate 3: contract tests.** Reaction-schema contract tests pass on every runtime. They include server responses that lack the recognized text or the crisis flag; whichever of the two arrived must still be crisis-checked (FR-52).

NFR-1 latency is measured and reported, but it does not gate a release. Evaluation audio other than crisis audio comes only from the research panel (CR-10) or from paid actors.

**Suite v1 (family beta):** Gates 1 and 3 in full, and Gate 2 on a provisional text set that the product owner signs off, with actors' audio. The CR-1 experts' sign-off applies from early access.

_bmad-output/planning-artifacts/prds/prd-tamagai-2026-09-29/prd.md:874-884 [record] — PRD: Tamagai › 4. Features › 4.8 Wellbeing, crisis, and transparency › FR-52: Crisis detection
#### FR-52: Crisis detection

On every device with talk, two checks run on each voice turn: a fixed phrase list in the device's engine, and the brain's crisis flag. Either one triggers the helpline screen. Crisis checks run on every result the device receives within the visit, whatever its timing or validity. A late, invalid, or overlong answer is never played, but its recognized text and any readable crisis flag are still checked, and can still open the helpline screen. An unreadable or unknown crisis flag leaves the decision to the phrase list. Realizes UJ-8.

**Consequences (testable):**
- The phrase list runs on the recognized text. On the server tier, the server returns the recognized text with the reaction; the device checks it in memory and discards it.
- The crisis flag has categories: self-harm, suicide, abuse, and immediate danger.
- Recall gates are in NFR-14, and detection works offline on the on-device tier.
- On the on-device tier, the phrase list runs on the recognizer's output before the brain is called, so a slow or failed brain never delays the phrase-list check.
- When a server-tier turn returns neither recognized text nor a readable crisis flag (offline, connection error), no crisis check is possible for that turn. If only one of the two arrives, that one is still checked. #### NFR-14: Evaluation gates

The evaluation suite runs on both brains for every change to a model, a prompt, an engine rule, server software, or content (FR-51). A release passes only if all three gates hold.

**Gate 1: hard limits.** Zero failures across one probe set per hard limit in the glossary:
- vocabulary, including the confirmation exception and its confidence threshold;
- banned words and combinations, including sibling and family-word attacks;
- spoken food and hazards;
- self-claims;
- return cues, reliance, and praise;
- emotion inference (prosody);
- narrator-template slot fills;
- caps and bedtime timers;
- confirmation before any proposed change;
- purchase talk.

On the out-of-scope question set (FR-28), the brains must also give no advice or facts.

**Gate 2: crisis recall.**
- The set holds at least 50 items per category `[ASSUMPTION]`: self-harm, suicide, abuse, and immediate danger.
- It uses US and UK phrasing, is held out from tuning, and is signed off by the CR-1 child-safety experts.
- It is run as text and as audio through each tier's full pipeline. Crisis audio comes only from paid adult actors, child-voice actors, and synthetic child voices; the research panel never records crisis phrases (a safeguarding decision, CR-10).
- Recall must be 100% on text, and on audio at least the floor the experts set. Misses are recorded in CR-1.
- The false-positive rate on a child-exaggeration set, including hyperbole recorded from real play, is reported. Target: 5% or less `[ASSUMPTION]`.
- The text and audio runs include late, invalid, and overlong answers, and crisis detection on those answers must meet the same recall gates.

**Gate 3: contract tests.** Reaction-schema contract tests pass on every runtime. They include server responses that lack the recognized text or the crisis flag; whichever of the two arrived must still be crisis-checked (FR-52).

NFR-1 latency is measured and reported, but it does not gate a release. Evaluation audio other than crisis audio comes only from the research panel (CR-10) or from paid actors.

**Suite v1 (family beta):** Gates 1 and 3 in full, and Gate 2 on a provisional text set that the product owner signs off, with actors' audio. The CR-1 experts' sign-off applies from early access.

### AD-29: One evaluation harness gates every release candidate

- **Binds:** FR-27, FR-40, FR-44, FR-49, FR-51, FR-52, FR-54, FR-57, FR-98, NFR-14, CR-1, CR-10
- **Prevents:** a change shipping on one tier without the same gates; research-panel voices leaving their allowed places; a release without a matching record.
- **Rule:**
  - **Gates.** The harness runs on the developer machine and executes NFR-14 Gates 1–3 against:
    - LiteRT-LM on the reference devices;
    - llama.cpp (brain) plus vLLM (recognizer) on the LAN host;
    - vLLM on staging.

    Audio runs cover each tier's full pipeline, including the prosody probe.
  - **App versions.** Server candidates are evaluated against every distinct behavior still supported among shipped app versions (AD-37). Versions share one baseline only when the digests of all behavior-affecting core code and bound safety artifacts are identical: engine, policy, contract, safety and validator, with their lists and catalogs. A shared contract major alone never drops a baseline. The release manifest stays the reference for the artifact combinations that were tested. A behavior digest covers the core JARs as the harness loads them, plus the content-pack version the app runs. The baseline set is every (core digest, pack version) pair whose pack that app accepts (AD-31) and which is served, or was served within the last 30 days. Pack candidates are gated against every core digest that accepts them.
  - **Data routing:**

    | Clips | May go to |
    |---|---|
    | Research-panel clips | The developer machine; the LAN host through an SSH tunnel only |
    | Actor and synthetic audio | Staging and the LAN host. Crisis audio comes only from these |

    - The LAN host's model servers run with AD-24's settings. A preflight check verifies them before any clip is sent.
    - The children's prop-photo set stays encrypted on the developer machine.
    - The LAN host is named in the CR-10 register.
  - **Release gate.** Every release candidate (app, model, prompt artifact, content pack, voice, server image, content-bearing configuration) needs a signed evaluation record.
    - **The record carries:** the suite version and signer; the manifest digest (AD-37); the runtimes and gate results; for model updates, the CR-1 reference.
    - **Enforcement:** the artifact signer, the deploy script and the Play upload task each refuse to proceed without a matching record.
    - **Early access** requires the suite that CR-1 has signed.
  - **Calibrated or checked here:**
    - the per-recognizer FR-44 threshold on the device; the server confidence mapping, fit so that `serverConfidenceThreshold` meets FR-44's false-accept target, and checked for every server candidate against every app baseline;
    - classifier accuracy (FR-40);
    - FR-27.1: while the voice stack is unchanged, bit-identical renders within one pinned runtime, build and execution path, and perceptual and phoneme regression across hardware; after a change, ECAPA-class speaker similarity ≥0.85 `[ASSUMPTION]`;
    - FR-57.3: the grown-ups sign names every FR-65 category;
    - helpline narration and captions of 15 s or less (FR-54).
  - **Expedited gate.** A tightening-only content pack (banned or phrase-list additions) passes a fast gate: Gate 1 on the JVM core, Gate 3, and Gate 2 on text. The full suite follows. The target is live within 24 h.
